A calculation worksheet is available online (Longcore et al., 2018b). 2.2.3.3.2 Plants and Vegetation Similar to the effects on wildlife, roadway lighting generally tends to have an effect on the plants that need a dark cycle to reach maturity, like soybeans. Roadway lighting has been shown to affect the growth and maturity of soybeans (Briggs, 2006; Palmer et al., 2017; Zong-Ming, 2007) and maize crops (Sinnadurai, 1981). The effects of LED roadway lighting on plant growth and maturity have not been reported yet; however, laboratory studies have shown that LEDs with higher blue content make soybean plants more compact (Cope & Bugbee, 2013). 2.2.4 Health and Well-being The impact of light on human health has been a significant field of investigation in recent years. Health and well-being benefits from reduced light pollution (e.g., improved sleep and being able to see the night sky) have been noted (House of Commons on Science and Technology, 2003; 27 Falchi, 2011). There are also putative benefits from reductions in artificial light at night, which have been linked to a range of health outcomes affected by disruptions to circadian rhythms (McFadden, 2014; Navara, 2007; Shuboni, 2010). 2.2.4.1 Physical Activity and Travel Mode Choice The impact of street lighting on the general population’s health and well-being is twofold. On one hand, there are negative impacts from light pollution or artificial light at night, which have been linked to a range of health outcomes affected by disruptions to the circadian rhythms and sleep as described in previous sections. On the other hand, street lighting has also been linked to physical activity, directly or indirectly, through perceived safety and security, although the associations are ambiguous. In different research projects, the self-reported presence of street lighting has produced both positive correlation to activity (Troped, 2003) as well as no association with activity (Eyler, 2003; King, 2000). In other research links were made with lighting and self-reports of activity using objectively defined geographic information system (GIS) measures (Duncan, 2005). 2.2.4.1.1 Walking Walking is one of the most common forms of physical activity, with documented benefits for health (Hu, 2001; Manson, 1999). Walking occurs primarily in neighborhood streets and public facilities (Lee, 2004), and the character of such places influences the degree to which they are safe, comfortable, and attractive for walking (Saelens, 2008). Improved street lighting is considered one of the effective practices in increasing walking and bicycling, along with other infrastructure improvements such as sidewalk quality, connectivity, and enhanced aesthetics at the street scale (Heath, 2006). Increasing light levels were found to be an influencing factor to promote the physical activity levels of the population, as shown by the increase in pedestrian and bicycle counts at night (Bhagavathula, 2017). Both walking and wheeling are low-cost, easy to implement forms of aerobic exercise, the recommendations for which almost half Americans do not meet (US Department of Health and Human Services, n.d.). 2.2.4.2 Mobility and Travel Mode Choice Steinbach (2015) suspected that reduced street lighting may lead to reduced mobility or changes
